section.title: Our Heavenly Dwelling
section.sectionRationale: Paul carries the hope of chapter four to its climax. If the outer self is wasting away, it is because the earthly tent in which we live is being dismantled, but we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven. So we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, that mortality may be swallowed up by life. God has prepared us for this and given the Spirit as a pledge. Therefore we walk by faith, not by sight, content to be away from the body and at home with the Lord, aiming to please Him, since we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
section.thesis: When the earthly tent of our body is dismantled we have an eternal dwelling from God; the Spirit is the pledge of that future, so we walk by faith and not by sight, longing to be at home with the Lord, and we aim to please Him because we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the earthly tent and the eternal house in heaven; the Spirit as the pledge that steadies faith over sight; and the confident aim to please the Lord before whose judgment seat we must all appear.

units.label: The tent and the eternal house
units.note: groaning to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling

verses.text: For we know that if the earthly {{skenos|tent}} we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.
For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling,
because when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.
For while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life.

units.label: The Spirit as pledge
units.note: we walk by faith, not by sight

verses.text: And it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the {{arrabon|Spirit as a pledge}} of what is to come.
Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord.
For we {{peripateo|walk}} by faith, not by sight.
We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
So we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it.
For we must all appear before the {{bema|judgment seat}} of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.

skenos.gloss: A tent or temporary dwelling, used as a figure for the mortal body. A tent is portable, fragile, and impermanent, fit for a pilgrim but not a lasting home. Paul contrasts it with a building from God, an eternal house not made by human hands. The imagery recalls Israel's wilderness tabernacle, a temporary tent later replaced by a permanent temple, and dignifies the body while pointing beyond it to the resurrection dwelling.

arrabon.gloss: A down payment, deposit, or pledge that guarantees the full payment to come. In commerce it was earnest money securing a transaction, the first instalment of what is certain to follow. God gives believers the Holy Spirit as this pledge, a real foretaste of the coming inheritance that guarantees the whole. The Spirit already at work in us is God's own guarantee that mortality will be swallowed up by life.

peripateo.gloss: To walk, and by extension to conduct one's whole life. Paul uses walking as a picture of the manner of life, the daily path a person treads. To walk by faith, not by sight, is to order the whole of life by trust in God's unseen promises rather than by what the eyes can measure. It describes a settled way of living, not an occasional act of believing.

bema.gloss: A raised platform or tribunal where a judge or magistrate rendered verdicts, the judgment seat. Every person must appear before the bema of Christ to receive what is due for the things done in the body. For the believer this is not a trial to determine salvation, which is secured in Christ, but an appearing before the Lord that assesses and rewards the life lived. It gives sober weight to how the present life is spent.

basic.context: Paul continues from chapter four, where the outer self is wasting away. He now explains why he does not lose heart in the face of death: the body is only a temporary tent, and when it is taken down the believer has an eternal house from God in heaven. So he groans, not to escape the body but to be further clothed with immortality, and God has given the Spirit as the guarantee of that hope. Confident even in the face of death, Paul aims above all to please the Lord, before whose judgment seat all must appear.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage speaks about death, the intermediate state, and resurrection, and Christians have discussed exactly how the pieces fit. The main thrust is clear: death is not the end for the believer but the doorway to being at home with the Lord and finally clothed with a resurrection body. Read the tent and house imagery as hope in the face of mortality, and verse 10 as the sober motivation to live for Christ now.
basic.originalLanguages: The body is a skenos, a tent, temporary and fragile, set against an eternal house from God. The Spirit is the arrabon, the down payment or pledge, guaranteeing the inheritance to come. We peripateo, walk, by faith, ordering all of life by trust rather than sight. And all must appear before the bema, the judgment seat, of Christ.
basic.typology: The tent recalls the wilderness tabernacle, a temporary dwelling later replaced by a permanent temple, picturing the mortal body giving way to the resurrection body. The longing for mortality to be swallowed up by life echoes the promise that death itself will be defeated, fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and the resurrection of His people.
basic.christ: Christ is the Lord to be at home with, the one whose presence is the believer's true dwelling. His resurrection is the guarantee and pattern of the eternal house not made by hands. He is the judge before whose seat all must appear, and yet for the believer He is the Saviour who has already secured their acceptance, so the judgment seat holds no condemnation but assesses a life lived for Him.
basic.god: God is the builder of the eternal house not made with hands, the one who has prepared His people for immortality and given the Spirit as the pledge of it. He is the God of resurrection hope, who purposes that mortality be swallowed up by life. The whole passage rests on His faithfulness to complete what He has begun.
basic.crossReferences: First Corinthians 15 unfolds the resurrection body that is imperishable. Romans 8 speaks of the whole creation and believers groaning as they await redemption. Philippians 1 expresses the desire to depart and be with Christ. Romans 14 says each will give account before God.
basic.oneStory: The account of redemption moves toward the defeat of death and the gift of resurrection life. Here Paul faces death with hope: the fragile tent of the body will be taken down, but an eternal house awaits, guaranteed by the Spirit. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and the final hope is not to be unclothed but clothed, mortality swallowed up by life in the resurrection.

context.literary:
The passage is one of the most compressed in Paul, and the key to reading it is its structure of three 'for' and 'so' links. Verse 1 begins with 'for' and states what Paul knows about the future. Verses 2 to 4 give the reason in terms of longing, each time opening with another 'for' or 'because.' Verse 5 steps back and names who has made this longing possible, and verses 6 to 10 draw the practical conclusion: so we are confident, so we walk by faith, so we aspire to please him.

The language is a dense run of paired images. The earthly tent stands against the eternal house, being unclothed against being clothed, mortality against life, being at home in the body against being at home with the Lord. The vocabulary of tents and clothing is mixed, with a building, a garment and a dwelling all serving the same idea, and Paul is not being careless. He is reaching for several pictures because none is adequate alone.

The verses stand at a hinge in the letter. The 'for' of verse 1 looks back to 4:17-18, where the outer self wastes away and the unseen is eternal, and the confidence of verse 6 echoes the 'we do not lose heart' of chapter 4. Verse 10 turns the discussion toward accountability, and verse 11 begins the argument about the ministry of reconciliation, in which 'the fear of the Lord' gives the next step its weight. Verse 7, 'we walk by faith, not by sight,' is a parenthesis that governs everything around it, because it explains how a person can be confident about things not yet seen.
context.historical:
Paul worked with his hands as a tentmaker, Acts 18:1-3, and had spent long hours cutting and stitching goat hair cloth. A tent was a familiar image of something light, portable and temporary, and Paul's readers in Corinth, many of whom would have known his trade, would hear in it the idea of a home that can be struck. Other Jewish and Christian writers could also speak of the body as a tent, as in 2 Peter 1:13-14, and Isaiah 38:12 has Hezekiah compare his life to a shepherd's tent pulled up.

The bema, the platform from which a magistrate delivered verdicts, was a feature of Roman civic life, and Corinth had one. It was in front of such a seat that Paul himself was brought by his opponents when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, Acts 18:12-17. The Corinthian readers could not hear 'the judgment seat' without remembering a very public place of accountability. At the same time the bema was also where awards were given at games, so the word could carry the sense of reward as well as of verdict.

Paul writes with death close. In 1:8-10 he said that in Asia he had felt the sentence of death, and in 4:7-12 he has described carrying the death of Jesus in his body. He was not speaking abstractly. He expected that he might die before the Lord returned, a possibility he had not allowed for in earlier letters, where the stress falls on being alive at the coming, 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and 1 Corinthians 15:51. In this letter he faces the other prospect and shows that it holds no terror.
context.canonical:
The passage draws on the Bible's long habit of speaking about God's dwelling. The tabernacle was a tent in which God lived among his people, and the temple replaced it as a house. The prophets, and then Jesus, spoke of a house 'not made with hands.' At his trial witnesses reported that Jesus had said he would destroy the man-made temple and build another made without hands, Mark 14:58, and John tells us he meant the temple of his body, John 2:19-21. Paul's language here belongs to that stream, in which the true dwelling of God is a person and a people, not a building.

The idea of a house waiting for believers finds its other statement in John 14:2-3, where Jesus tells his disciples that there are many rooms in his Father's house and that he will come back to take them to himself. Hebrews 9:11 uses the same adjective 'not made by hands' of the true tabernacle through which Christ entered. At the other end of the Bible, Revelation 21:3 announces that the dwelling place of God is with man.

The thread of resurrection runs through the passage. 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 uses the same clothing language of putting on the imperishable and the same quotation about death swallowed up, from Isaiah 25:8. Romans 8:22-23 describes the same groaning, and Philippians 1:21-24 offers Paul's own longing to depart and be with Christ. Together these passages show the shape of Christian hope: a body raised, a presence with Christ in the meantime, and a final dwelling in the new creation. The judgment seat finds a parallel in Romans 14:10-12 and in the testing of works in 1 Corinthians 3:10-15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to hold two truths together, that bodily life is temporary and that its end is not a disaster. Having spoken of an outer self that is wasting away, he does not want them to conclude that the Christian hope is only a better version of survival. He wants them to see that death has already been defeated in principle and that what follows is not a loss but a gain.

He also wants them to hear the groaning as a sign of life. The longing he describes is not despair but the expectation of a person who knows a better home is waiting, and who therefore finds the present one limiting. The Spirit already given is evidence that the promise is real, so the longing has a basis.

Finally, he wants them to take the judgment seat seriously. The comfort of the passage is not a reason to be careless. Because the Lord before whom all will appear is the same Lord with whom the believer wishes to be at home, the proper response is to aim to please him now, whether in the body or out of it. The structure of the passage keeps hope and responsibility together, and Paul presses both so that his readers will neither cling to this life in fear nor drift through it in carelessness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the passage is description of Paul's own settled outlook, and it should not be turned into a detailed map of what happens at death. Paul says that he would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord, but he does not give a timetable or a description of the intermediate condition. The passage describes his confidence and the ground of it. Readers go beyond the text when they insist on details it does not supply.

The statement about groaning is also descriptive. It records what Paul and his companions feel, and it explains why the longing is not a sign of weak faith. It should not be read as an instruction to wish for death, as though the believer were to be impatient to leave. In Philippians 1:24 the same man says that remaining in the body is needed for the sake of others.

What is prescribed is spelled out in verses 7 and 9: walk by faith, not by sight, and aspire to please the Lord. These are instructions for the present, and they hold whatever one's view of the intermediate state. The verse about the judgment seat is a statement of fact about every person, and it is applied as a motive. It is not a threat that salvation can be lost, since verse 10 is about what each person receives for what was done in the body and Romans 8:1 says that there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.

debates.question: When does the believer receive the heavenly dwelling, at death or at the resurrection?

views.label: At the final resurrection
views.case: Many read the eternal house as the resurrection body received at Christ's return, so that between death and resurrection the believer is with the Lord but awaits the final clothing, consistent with First Corinthians 15.

views.label: Received at or from the moment of death
views.case: Others argue the believer is clothed with the heavenly dwelling immediately at death, avoiding any nakedness, reading verses 1 to 4 to mean there is no gap of unclothed existence.

debates.bearing: Both agree that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord and that resurrection glory is certain; the passage gives comfort in death whichever way the timing is understood.

debates.question: What is the intermediate state Paul describes as being away from the body and at home with the Lord?

views.label: Conscious presence with Christ
views.case: The historic Christian reading is that at death the believer is consciously present with the Lord, awaiting the resurrection of the body, matching Philippians 1 and the promise to the thief on the cross.

views.label: An unwelcome nakedness to be avoided
views.case: Some stress Paul's reluctance to be unclothed, taking his longing as directed past any intermediate state to the resurrection body itself, so the emphasis falls on the final clothing.

debates.bearing: Either way the believer's hope is sure: death cannot separate from the Lord, and the goal is the resurrection life in which mortality is swallowed up.

debates.question: What is the judgment seat of Christ for the believer?

views.label: An assessment and reward of the believer's life, not a trial for salvation
views.case: Since believers are justified in Christ, the bema evaluates and rewards how the redeemed lived, without placing salvation in doubt, consistent with First Corinthians 3.

views.label: A solemn appearing that includes all people
views.case: Others stress the universal scope, that all must appear and receive their due, holding together sober accountability with the security of those in Christ.

debates.bearing: For the believer the judgment seat is not condemnation but a real accounting that gives weight to present obedience, motivating a life aimed at pleasing the Lord.

study.originalLanguages:
The tent of verse 1 is skenos, a word that in the Greek Old Testament is close to the tabernacle's own vocabulary, and the Greek for 'dismantled' is kataluo, to take apart or loosen. The same verb is used in the Gospels of the destruction of the temple, Mark 14:58 and Matthew 26:61, which helps explain why Paul's image has a temple resonance. The house is oikodome, a building, and the adjective 'not made by hands' is acheiropoietos. It appears in Mark 14:58 of the temple Jesus would raise and in Colossians 2:11 of circumcision done by Christ, and in each case it marks something that is God's own work and not a human product.

The verb for 'we have' in verse 1 is in the present tense: echomen, 'we have.' That tense is one source of the debate about timing. It can be a present possession in promise, a statement that the house is certain, or a description of what happens at death. The tense alone does not settle the matter, since Paul regularly uses the present for things that are sure.

The clothing language moves between two verbs. In verses 2 and 4 the word for 'be clothed' is a compound form, ependusasthai, which means to be clothed over or to put on over, and the plain verb endusasthai appears in verse 3. Paul uses the same plain verb in 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 for putting on the imperishable. The point of verse 4 is that he does not want to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life. The verb for 'swallowed up' is katapino, the same word that appears in 1 Corinthians 15:54, where Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8. In both places death is the thing swallowed.

The pledge of verse 5, arrabon, is a commercial word for a down payment that binds the giver to complete the purchase. The Greek version of Genesis 38:17-18 uses it of the pledge Judah left with Tamar until he paid. Paul uses it for the Spirit here and in 1:22, and Ephesians 1:14 does the same. The Spirit is a first instalment of the same kind as what will follow.

Verses 6 and 8 use a pair of verbs about being at home. Endemeo means to be at home, and ekdemeo means to be away from home. They are used of the body and the Lord alternately, so that being at home in the body means being away from the Lord, and the reverse. Paul does not say that the body is a prison, but that the believer's true home is where Christ is. In verse 9 the verb translated 'aspire' is philotimeomai, to make it one's ambition or to love honour, which shows that the desire to please God is to be as strong as any worldly ambition. And in verse 10 the bema stands at the end, with phanerothenai, 'to be made manifest,' as the verb: the point of the judgment is that what has been done in the body will be fully revealed.

typology.type: The tabernacle as a tent of dwelling, Exodus 25:8-9
typology.fulfillment: God told Moses to make a sanctuary so that he might dwell among his people, and for centuries the dwelling was a tent that could be moved. Paul says that the body is also a tent, that it will be struck, and that a permanent house from God waits. In Christ the correspondence deepens: the Word 'tabernacled' among us, John 1:14, and the temple he spoke of was his own body, John 2:19-21. The type falls short only in that it concerned a place, whereas the fulfilment is a person raised and a people clothed in a resurrection life.

typology.type: The temple made without hands, Mark 14:58
typology.fulfillment: The charge at Jesus' trial was that he would destroy the temple made by hands and build another not made by hands. John records that he meant his body, which would be raised on the third day. Paul takes the phrase 'not made by hands' and uses it of the believer's future dwelling. The resurrection of Christ is both the pattern and the source of the house that awaits. Believers are also described as the temple of the Spirit in the present, 1 Corinthians 6:19, so the type is already partly true, and its completion is the resurrection body.

typology.type: Clothing as a sign of God's covering, Genesis 3:21
typology.fulfillment: After the fall God made garments for the man and woman and clothed them, covering a nakedness that had become shame. Paul's talk of being clothed and not found naked in verses 3 and 4 echoes that picture, though the text does not cite Genesis. The final clothing is a body fit for God's presence, in which the exposed and the mortal are covered by life. The type is partial, since Genesis speaks of covering shame and Paul speaks of overcoming death, and it should be heard as a resonance and not as an argument.

typology.type: The pledge and the firstfruits, Romans 8:23
typology.fulfillment: Israel presented the first of the harvest to the LORD as a promise of the whole. Paul speaks of the 'firstfruits of the Spirit' in Romans 8:23, and in this passage he calls the Spirit a pledge. In both places the thing given now is a real part of the future gift. The Spirit does not stand in for the inheritance but is its beginning, and the day the redemption of the body arrives the pledge will be redeemed in full, Ephesians 1:14.

study.christ:
Christ is not named often in these ten verses, but the passage is full of him. The eternal house is from God through the one who was raised. The Spirit given as a pledge is the Spirit of the risen Lord. The home to which Paul looks is 'with the Lord,' and the judgment before which all will stand is the judgment seat 'of Christ.' Every movement of the passage ends in him.

The resurrection is the ground of the hope. Paul says that we know we have a building from God, and the knowing rests on what has happened to Jesus. The temple he spoke of, his body, was destroyed and raised, John 2:19-21, and the body he now has is the pattern of ours. Philippians 3:20-21 says that the Lord Jesus Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body. 1 Corinthians 15:45 calls him the life giving spirit and the last Adam. The eternal house is the share in his risen life.

Christ is the one with whom the believer will be at home. Paul's preference to be away from the body is not a preference for non existence or for a state of bare freedom but for his presence. Philippians 1:23 says the same, 'to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed,' and Jesus promised the thief on the cross that he would be with him in Paradise that day, Luke 23:43. John 14:3 gives the promise in the Lord's own words: he will welcome his people into his presence so that they may be where he is. The comfort of death for the believer is entirely a comfort about a person.

Christ is also the judge. Verse 10 is a fact about every human being, not only unbelievers, and Paul asserts that it is Christ's seat. That is a sobering thought, and it is meant to be. But the judge is the one who died for the people who stand before him. Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in him, and John 5:24 says that whoever hears his word and believes has crossed from death to life and does not come under judgment. The judgment seat of verse 10 is not a second trial of salvation but an assessment of the life lived in the body, and its Judge is the Saviour. Paul will say in verse 21 that Christ became sin for us, which makes the seat a place where the verdict has already been secured.

A caution applies. Not every image should be pressed into a fixed doctrine about Christ. The tent and the house are metaphors, and the text does not say whether they are literal descriptions of an intermediate or a final body. What it does say clearly is that the believer's future is bound to Christ and that nothing in death can separate the believer from him.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the builder. The house is 'from God,' verse 1, and it is 'not built by human hands.' Everything that matters most for the believer's future is a work of God and not of human effort. The body will be taken apart and nothing we can do will stop it, but God has made another dwelling ready, and the promise rests on his faithfulness.

He is the God who prepares. Verse 5 says that 'God has prepared us for this very purpose.' The preparation is in the present: it is the work he is already doing in the believer, as in 4:16, where the inner self is being renewed day by day. This is a God who does not leave people to face death unprepared, and who has been shaping them for resurrection long before it comes.

He is the God who keeps his pledge. He gives the Spirit as a down payment, and a down payment binds the giver. The Spirit is the sign that God's own character is on the line, so that the believer's hope rests on God's integrity. Ephesians 1:13-14 and 2 Corinthians 1:21-22 say the same: God has sealed his people and given the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.

He is the God of life. The aim of the longing is that mortality 'may be swallowed up by life,' and it is God who gives that life. The reading of Isaiah 25:8 behind verse 4, where the Lord swallows death forever, shows that this is the God who makes an end of death and who will wipe away the tears from every face. Death is not his equal opponent. It is his creature, and it will be undone.

He is also a God who judges. Verse 10 says that each will receive what is due, 'good or bad.' God's justice is not suspended by his mercy. It is the justice of one who takes the things done in the body seriously, because the body and what is done in it matter to him. Romans 2:6 says that he repays each one according to his deeds, and the fact that this is said of believers as well as others in verse 10 shows that his holiness reaches his own people. Yet the same God has put them in Christ, so judgment and mercy are held together without being blurred.

For worship, the passage teaches us to praise God for what he has already given, the Spirit, and for what he has promised. It teaches confidence without arrogance, since the confidence is in him. And it teaches us to bring our fear of death to him, to groan honestly, and to ask him to complete what he has begun.

crossReferences.note: The perishable must put on the imperishable and the mortal immortality, and then death is swallowed up in victory. It uses the same clothing and swallowing images as 2 Corinthians 5:2-4 and shows that both passages are speaking of the same hope in different words.

The Lord will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from every face. It is the Old Testament source of the phrase about mortality being swallowed up by life, and it shows that Paul's hope is not private speculation but the fulfilment of a prophetic promise.

The whole creation groans, and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit also groan inwardly as they wait for the redemption of the body. It is the closest parallel to the groaning in verses 2 and 4, and it shows that the longing is shared with all creation and not just a personal sentiment.

To live is Christ and to die is gain. Paul is torn between departing to be with Christ, which is far better, and remaining for the sake of others. It gives the personal side of 2 Corinthians 5:8, and shows that the preference to be with the Lord is balanced by service.

Jesus speaks of destroying the temple and raising it in three days, and the writer explains that he was speaking of the temple of his body. It grounds Paul's language of a dwelling not made by hands in the resurrection of Christ, whose body is the pattern of the eternal house.

In the Father's house are many rooms, and Jesus will come and welcome his people into his presence. It is the Lord's own statement of the hope Paul describes, and it shows that the destination of verse 8 is a person and a place prepared by him.

We will all stand before God's judgment seat, and each of us will give an account to God. It uses the same image as verse 10 and states it in the context of how believers treat one another, which shows that the judgment seat is meant to shape present conduct.

Each builder's work will be tested by fire, and if it survives he receives a reward, while if it is burned he suffers loss but is himself saved. It sheds light on what receiving one's due in verse 10 means for believers: the work is assessed, and the person is secure.

Believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of the inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession. It uses the same word for pledge as 2 Corinthians 5:5, and shows that the Spirit is the guarantee that points toward the day of final redemption.

Our citizenship is in heaven, and the Saviour will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body. It states the end result that Paul longs for in the image of clothing: a body made like Christ's, so that the unclothed state is not the goal and the clothing over is.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a man formed from dust and given the breath of life, and it carries from the start the sentence that follows the fall: to dust you shall return, Genesis 3:19. Death comes into the world through sin, and every later part of the Bible tells how God deals with it. This passage sits at a point near the end of that story, where the answer has been given and the believer waits for it to be completed.

The Old Testament carries the hope in pieces. Job says that after his skin is destroyed he will see God in his flesh, Job 19:26, Isaiah promises that God will swallow up death forever, Isaiah 25:8, and Daniel says that many who sleep in the dust will awake, Daniel 12:2. None of these tells how, and none gives a face to the one who will bring it about. In Christ they find their answer, because he died and was raised on the third day, and his resurrection is the first fruits of the harvest, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

This passage is where that victory is applied to a believer who is aging, suffering and expecting to die. The tent is real, and the groaning is real, but so is the house. It teaches that the Christian's last enemy has already been beaten, that the Spirit is the first part of the payment, and that being with Christ is better than anything this life offers. It also teaches that the story is not only about the future. The judgment seat means that how we live now has weight.

The new creation completes the picture. The end of the Bible is not souls floating free of bodies but a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with his people, Revelation 21:1-3, and death is no more. The tent has been replaced by a permanent dwelling, and in a deeper sense the tabernacle that began in the wilderness has come to rest. The people who once groaned in the tent will live in the house, and the longing of this passage will have been answered by the presence of God himself.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by the earthly tent that is dismantled?

options.text: The mortal body, which is temporary, over against an eternal house from God.
options.note: Verse 1 contrasts the fragile tent of the body with a permanent building from God.

options.text: The physical church building where they met.
options.note: The tent is a figure for the body, not a meeting place.

options.text: The city of Corinth that would soon fall.
options.note: Paul speaks of the individual body, not a city.

options.text: The old covenant system of worship.
options.note: The tent here is the mortal body, not the old covenant.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call the Spirit a pledge?

options.text: The Spirit is God's down payment guaranteeing the full inheritance of resurrection life to come.
options.note: Verse 5 uses arrabon, a deposit that secures what is certain to follow.

options.text: The Spirit is only a temporary gift until Christ returns.
options.note: The Spirit is a real foretaste and guarantee, not a mere placeholder.

options.text: Believers pledge the Spirit back to God as a promise.
options.note: It is God who gives the Spirit as His pledge to us, not the reverse.

options.text: The Spirit is a symbol with no real presence now.
options.note: The Spirit is genuinely given and at work as the guarantee of glory.

quiz.q: What does it mean to walk by faith, not by sight?

options.text: To order the whole of life by trust in God's unseen promises rather than what the eyes can measure.
options.note: Verse 7 describes a settled way of living governed by faith in unseen realities.

options.text: To make decisions with no thought or wisdom at all.
options.note: Faith is not thoughtlessness; it trusts God's promises rather than mere appearances.

options.text: To expect visible miracles to guide every step.
options.note: It is precisely trusting when we cannot see, not demanding sight.

options.text: To ignore the physical world as unreal.
options.note: Paul affirms the body and resurrection; he is not denying the physical.

quiz.q: What is the judgment seat of Christ for the believer?

options.text: An appearing before the Lord that assesses and rewards the life lived, not a trial that decides salvation.
options.note: Verse 10 speaks of receiving one's due, while salvation rests secure in Christ.

options.text: A trial to determine whether the believer is finally saved.
options.note: Salvation is secured in Christ; the bema assesses the redeemed life.

options.text: A formality with no bearing on how we live now.
options.note: It gives sober weight to present obedience, aiming to please the Lord.
Paul says we must all appear before it.

questions: Paul faces death as the taking down of a tent, with an eternal house waiting. How does that picture change the way you think about your own mortality?
The Spirit is God's pledge guaranteeing the glory to come. When your hope feels thin, how does it help to know you already have a real foretaste of the future?
To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. Does your hope of heaven centre on being with Christ Himself, or on something less?
We walk by faith, not by sight. Where are you tempted to live by what you can see rather than by God's unseen promises?
Paul aims to please the Lord because we must all appear before His judgment seat. How would living with that day in view reshape your choices this week?

translationNotes.note: The earthly tent renders skenos, a temporary dwelling used figuratively for the mortal body, set against a permanent building from God, the resurrection dwelling.
The word rendered pledge is arrabon, a commercial down payment guaranteeing full payment; the Spirit is the first instalment and guarantee of the coming inheritance.

The judgment seat renders bema, a raised tribunal; for the believer it is an appearing that assesses and rewards the life lived rather than a trial that determines salvation, which is secured in Christ.
